title: The Soviet Union invades eastern Poland
subtitle: The second invasion and the closing roads
body:
Before dawn on 17 September 1939, the Soviet government attempted to deprive its forthcoming invasion of a legally recognisable opponent. The note presented to Polish ambassador Wacław Grzybowski asserted that the Polish state and government had ceased to exist; he refused to accept it. Poland’s capital was still resisting, its armies remained in the field and its government had not yet left the country. The discrepancy between the note and these circumstances directs attention to the invasion’s central political mechanism: Moscow invoked the disappearance of Polish authority to justify an action that would further destroy its capacity to function. The note presented to Grzybowski made the Soviet argument in a carefully arranged sequence. Poland’s government had broken down; the state had consequently ceased to exist; agreements with that state had therefore lost their force. Ukrainians and Belarusians in eastern Poland supposedly required protection, and the Red Army would provide it. The American ambassador’s contemporary report preserves this explanation as Moscow issued it. It records a justification for an invasion, not an impartial account of conditions in Poland. [1] [2] For Polish soldiers and civilians, the practical question was more immediate. Much of the country was already exposed to the German offensive described in the [previous study](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01). The east contained military depots, replacement units, roads towards neutral neighbours and people who had fled the fighting farther west. Soviet intervention brought another army into this remaining space. It threatened the possibility of regrouping, but also the simpler hope that continuing eastward would lead a family away from the war. The [agreement of 23 August](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23) established the diplomatic framework for partition. September’s correspondence discloses the additional work needed to turn that framework into an invasion: arranging timing, limiting the risk of encounters between aircraft and troops, and negotiating the language in which cooperation would be presented. Polish decisions developed within a different information environment, as commanders assessed resistance, evacuation and surrender with damaged communications. The chapter follows the connection between this planned intervention and the uncertainty imposed on those who had to respond to it.

A pretext prepared in advance

Moscow’s public explanation was being discussed with Germany a week before Soviet troops crossed the border. On 10 September, Foreign Commissar Vyacheslav Molotov told the German ambassador, Friedrich-Werner von der Schulenburg, that the speed of Germany’s advance had surprised the Soviet leadership. Military preparations had to be accelerated. Molotov also explained the political story he intended to tell: Poland was collapsing, and the Soviet Union must protect Ukrainians and Belarusians threatened by Germany. According to Schulenburg’s report, Molotov considered that explanation necessary to keep the intervention from appearing aggressive. [3] The conversation links political justification directly to operational preparation. Molotov considered the protective explanation while the forces for intervention were still being made ready, and expressed concern that a German–Polish armistice would make Soviet entry appear to initiate another war. His reasoning, as Schulenburg reported it, treated the form of the announcement as a problem to be solved alongside military timing. It provides unusually direct evidence that the subsequent language of necessity was being constructed in anticipation of action. On 14 September, Molotov said that military action could begin sooner than previously expected, but he wanted to know when Warsaw would fall. The capital’s capture would strengthen the claim that Poland had ceased to function. Soviet newspapers were already preparing the political explanation. Warsaw, however, continued to resist. The invasion would go ahead without the event that Moscow had hoped to use as its most convincing evidence. [4] Berlin wanted Soviet intervention, but objected to being cast as the danger from which the Red Army was rescuing its neighbours. On 15 September, Joachim von Ribbentrop instructed Schulenburg to explain that such language would present the two governments as enemies. His message also pressed for the date and hour of Soviet entry and for arrangements between military representatives. Germany’s interest was practical as well as political: Soviet action could spare German forces the task of pursuing the remaining Polish armies all the way towards the Soviet frontier. [5] At about two in the morning on 17 September, Stalin received Schulenburg with Molotov and Defence Commissar Kliment Voroshilov present. He announced that Soviet forces would cross that morning. The discussion included a proposed limit for German aircraft along the Białystok–Brest–Lwów line, intended to reduce the danger of clashes between the advancing armies. Stalin also read the diplomatic note intended for Poland and, according to the German report, altered three passages after Schulenburg objected. The telegram does not preserve the discarded wording; it does establish that Germany had an opportunity to influence the explanation before Poland received it. [6]

The production of an official explanation

Stalin revised the joint communiqué

Hilger’s memorandum of 18 September records a second process of revision, separate from the earlier changes to the note addressed to Poland. The German draft proposed a new territorial and economic order. Stalin judged its language excessively candid and supplied another text, whose publication required Berlin’s assent. The two drafts survive as enclosures. Their differences allow the historian to examine the preparation of the public explanation, while Hilger’s account remains a German diplomatic record rather than an independent transcript of Stalin’s intentions.

[7]
The private correspondence identifies compatible immediate purposes: Moscow would occupy its agreed sphere while Polish resistance to Germany continued, and Berlin would accommodate the Soviet advance. Cooperation took practical forms through advance notice, military contacts and attempts to prevent unintended clashes. It did not require the two governments to relinquish their separate interests or create a single command. This limited but consequential coordination was already developing before Poland received the assertion that intervention had become necessary because its state no longer existed.

Orders, formations and directions

The military instructions make the planning visible. Directives 16633 and 16634, issued on 14 September over the names of Voroshilov and Chief of the General Staff Boris Shaposhnikov, ordered secret concentration, readiness by the end of 16 September and an offensive across the frontier at dawn on the 17th. They assigned commanders, forces, successive objectives and deadlines. Their language concerned defeating opposing troops. These were orders for an invasion, already prepared before the protective explanation was delivered. [8] [9] The northern offensive developed under the Byelorussian Front, commanded by Mikhail Kovalyov; the southern offensive under Semyon Timoshenko’s Ukrainian Front. A Soviet front was a command directing several armies across a broad theatre. The surviving orders are especially useful because they identify seven operational groups by their concentration areas. Those names allow us to follow the original assignments without treating later changes in army organisation as though they had all been settled in the same document. The map therefore retains the group names used in the 14 September instructions. [10] The northern groups received objectives towards Wilno, Grodno and Baranowicze, while the southern groups were assigned approaches through Volhynia towards Lwów and the Romanian frontier. The orders combined rifle and cavalry divisions with tank formations, giving mobile forces a role in reaching beyond the immediate frontier and obstructing Polish reorganisation. Those assignments depended on infantry, artillery and supply following the leading elements. The schematic directions on the map should accordingly be read as the projected movement of combined forces, with subsequent occupation requiring further action.

The deadlines reveal the anticipated tempo more honestly than a single claim about kilometres advanced per day. The southern order expected the Shepetovka group around Równe and Dubno by the end of 17 September and at Łuck on the following day. Golikov’s group was given successive lines on the approach to Lwów. Tyulenev’s was directed towards the Strypa and then Stanisławów, with the wider purpose of cutting escape routes. These were ambitious marching and fighting schedules, dependent on roads remaining usable and resistance being overcome or bypassed. They cannot be converted into confirmed daily front lines. [9]

Reading the atlas

An arrow can show an intention

Open the 17 September map to see the seven planned directions. The lines are deliberately schematic. Their endpoints identify the direction of later objectives; they do not mean that Soviet troops stood there on the first evening. Front labels identify command sectors, not headquarters. The battles discussed below occurred over the following fortnight and remain dated separately in the campaign chronology.

The Polish decision: fight, withdraw, or preserve the army

Reports of resistance reached foreign capitals almost immediately. On the morning of 17 September, the Polish ambassador in Paris told American ambassador William Bullitt that Soviet forces had entered northeastern Poland and that Polish troops were fighting them. The report is valuable precisely because it preceded the later simplifications. Border units did not all watch the invasion pass unopposed. News was arriving from separate places, through a state whose communications were damaged but whose diplomats and soldiers were still acting. [11] Marshal Edward Rydz-Śmigły’s response attempted to preserve what remained of Poland’s armed forces. He directed a general withdrawal towards Romania and Hungary and instructed troops to avoid combat with the Soviets unless attacked or subjected to disarmament. That qualification was crucial. The order was neither an invitation to join the Red Army nor an unconditional instruction to surrender. It sought to prevent an already hard-pressed army from exhausting itself against another vastly superior opponent while routes out of the country might still be available. [2] The instruction to preserve the army left commanders to judge circumstances that could change during an encounter. A Soviet demand for disarmament threatened a unit’s capacity to continue the war, while resistance might expose it to encirclement or close an escape route. Withdrawal could preserve trained men but surrender the crossing or town that protected other troops. The decisions at Grodno, Lwów and among the Border Protection Corps consequently differed because their operational circumstances differed. Treating all of them as obedience or disobedience to one simple national policy obscures the discretion forced upon commanders by the invasion. The government’s movement into Romania during the night of 17–18 September came after the Soviet invasion had begun. Its departure therefore cannot explain an attack publicly justified before it happened. Nor did crossing a frontier automatically extinguish the state or the allegiance of its armed forces. The immediate result was nevertheless disastrous for command: leaders attempting to continue their work abroad instead faced internment, while soldiers still inside Poland had to act amid rapidly narrowing options. Poland’s political and military continuation would have to be rebuilt outside the country. [12] The same reversal confronted refugees. People who had travelled east to escape Germany now found that their destination was becoming another occupied zone. The Holocaust Memorial Museum describes a flight conducted with whatever transport was available and often without a settled plan for where to stop. That uncertainty is worth preserving in the narrative. Families were not moving across the finished occupation map familiar to later readers; they were trying to determine which road was still open, where relatives might be found and whether the next border could be crossed. [13] Warsaw’s continuing resistance was conspicuous evidence against the Soviet account, but the issue extended beyond the capital’s survival. Loss of territory and communications reduced the Polish government’s effective power without extinguishing its claim to govern or the allegiance of its forces. Soviet military instructions addressed those forces as opponents to be defeated while diplomacy challenged the existence of the state they served. The invasion thus combined a campaign against remaining military capacity with an attempt to delegitimise continued Polish resistance.

Where the advance met resistance

Wilno was fought over on 18–19 September. Grodno’s resistance followed on 20–22 September, with the principal fighting on the first two days and withdrawal continuing into the third. These dates matter because they show the invasion developing over time. Cities did not become Soviet possessions merely because they lay beyond the first frontier crossings. In each place, decisions about evacuation and defence intersected with the arrival of mobile Soviet forces. [2] Grodno illustrates the weakness concealed by a fast armoured approach. Much of its regular garrison had already been sent elsewhere. Major Benedykt Serafin helped organise a defence drawing on remaining servicemen and volunteers. On 20 September, tanks of the Soviet 27th Tank Brigade entered across the Niemen bridge without sufficient infantry support. Polish defenders used the weapons available, including petrol bottles at close range. Tanks inside streets could be attacked from positions their crews had difficulty seeing or reaching. Soviet reinforcements made the struggle increasingly unequal, and the main Polish forces withdrew during the night of 21–22 September. [14] The withdrawal led to further fighting near Kodziowce during the night of 21–22 September. The Polish 101st Reserve Uhlan Regiment, commanded by Major Stanisław Żukowski, encountered a Soviet mobile detachment associated with the 2nd Tank Brigade. The episode belongs to the history of cavalry operating against armour, but should not be reduced to a contest between a horse and a tank. It was a confused fight involving movement through villages and darkness, with Polish units trying to keep a route towards the Lithuanian frontier open. [15]

A soldier’s field of view

Three kilometres from a battle

Lieutenant Piotr Łazarewicz recorded that his exhausted company slept until seven on 22 September, unaware of fighting about three kilometres away. When it moved towards prepared trenches, those defences faced the Germans. His diary brings the campaign down to the scale of an officer receiving fragments of news, looking for cover and waiting for a messenger. His account of enemy losses came from another officer; it is not an independently checked tally. [12]

Farther south, General Wilhelm Orlik-Rückemann gathered surviving Border Protection Corps units into an improvised force. At Szack on 28–29 September, Polish troops fought their way through Soviet opposition, using concealed 37-mm antitank guns against approaching armour. Success opened a route towards the Bug, but it did not solve exhaustion, supply shortages or the danger beyond the next crossing. At Wytyczno on 1 October, renewed fighting ended with the decision to disperse the worn-down formation. The Polish Army Museum’s account follows this progression from concentration to tactical success and eventual dissolution. [16]

Lwów and the value of a promise

Lwów confronted the Soviet advance while already defending itself against Germany. German attempts to seize the city had begun on 12 September and met resistance. On 18 September, the armoured trains Śmiały and Bartosz Głowacki reached the city; Soviet forward units attacked during the following night and were repulsed. The arrival of Śmiały provides a tangible connection with the first invasion study, where the train supported the fighting at Mokra. Equipment and men were still moving through Poland, even as the space in which they could operate contracted. [17] German forces subsequently withdrew from around Lwów under the arrangements between the occupying powers. For the defenders, that movement did not restore a secure rear or end the siege. It changed the immediate opponent with whom the city’s fate would be negotiated. General Władysław Langner accepted terms on 22 September that promised personal liberty and freedom of movement to Polish officers and protection of civilian property. Soviet authorities then violated those assurances and took Polish servicemen into captivity. [17] The surrender terms need to be assessed within the information available to Langner. Continued fighting entailed responsibility for soldiers and civilians with diminishing prospects of relief, whereas the offered guarantees appeared to provide a way to limit further destruction. Their subsequent breach does not retrospectively remove that decision’s uncertainty. It instead identifies the coercive advantage obtained when the receiving authority accepted a surrender on assurances it then failed to honour. The episode connects the conduct of operations to the obligations that arose when combatants entered captivity. Elsewhere, Soviet conquest also brought executions, arrests and the seizure of people associated with Polish authority. The Institute of National Remembrance documents killings of prisoners and defenders, including after the fighting at Grodno, alongside the developing machinery of detention. These actions were part of the immediate occupation, not merely consequences of later policies. The fate of captured officers would eventually lead into the history of the special camps and the Katyn murders of 1940; this study ends before that later crime, while recognising the connection created by captivity in September. [18]

Soldiers, civilians and incompatible expectations

Soviet soldiers entered Poland under instructions that described the operation as liberation from national and class oppression. Yet official language did not produce a single private response. A study published by the Institute of National Remembrance draws on Soviet political and police reporting to show enthusiasm, uncertainty and dissent. One recorded question from an officer before the invasion was whether sympathy should now lie with Poland or Germany. Such remarks reveal the difficulty of absorbing the sudden diplomatic turn; surveillance reports, however, cannot tell us how representative any particular opinion was. [19]

A changing explanation

Simonov’s remembered reaction

Konstantin Simonov later recalled sympathy for Poland when Germany attacked and then approval of Soviet intervention when it was presented as protection for threatened populations. He was a young correspondent in Mongolia, not an eyewitness to the Polish frontier crossings. His retrospective account is useful as one person’s recollection of how the official explanation could reconcile apparently conflicting feelings. It should not be treated as the voice of every Soviet soldier. [19]

Among civilians, national identity alone cannot explain every reaction. Eastern Poland contained communities divided by language, religion, property, politics and relations with the Polish state. Some people welcomed the incoming army; others hid, fled, resisted or waited to see what would happen. Stanisław Boridczenko’s study of Polish military accounts from Polesie and Volhynia finds sharply different reactions in neighbouring localities. It also emphasises how officers’ assumptions and retrospective memories shaped what they recorded. Reports of attacks on Polish troops are evidence of particular acts, not a licence to assign collective guilt to an entire population. [20] One episode in that scholarship concerns the evacuation of military families from Pińsk to Dawidgródek. Orlik-Rückemann’s subsequent report described the move as protection from local hostility and judged that it had succeeded. The difference between two nearby places mattered more immediately to those families than a broad ethnic label. Other testimony distinguished violent armed groups from inhabitants who condemned them. The region contained collaboration, intimidation and assistance, sometimes close together; the invasion changed who could act openly and who needed protection. [20] Christoph Mick’s comparison of Polish, Ukrainian and Jewish experiences in Lwów places conflicting memories within their different social and political circumstances. Its methodological implication is that a city cannot be assigned a single collective response to occupation. Testimony about welcome, fear, assistance or hostility must be located in the witness’s situation and considered alongside evidence from other inhabitants. Such comparison explains the coexistence of divergent experiences without allowing one account to stand for every person who lived through the change of power. [21] Jewish refugees faced a particularly dangerous comparison between the power they were escaping and the power arriving from the east. Flight from Nazi persecution could make Soviet entry appear to offer immediate safety, without implying approval of Soviet rule. Later arrests and deportations also affected Jewish refugees in the Soviet zone. The Holocaust Memorial Museum’s account follows people who remained in the Soviet zone, tried to cross another frontier or were subsequently deported into the Soviet interior. Decisions that look contradictory on a finished map become more comprehensible when separation, poverty and uncertain information are restored to the story. [13]

Foreign obligations, refugees and recognition

Polish diplomacy had no difficulty identifying the Soviet action as aggression. On the evening of 17 September, Bullitt reported that Poland’s ambassador in Paris had received Foreign Minister Józef Beck’s denunciation of the invasion. The ambassador also expressed bitter disappointment at the lack of effective British and French help and deep pessimism about Romania’s willingness to act. This was the view from a diplomatic post trying to obtain assistance while the military situation deteriorated faster than allied discussions could change it. [22] In London, the next day’s conversation between American ambassador Joseph Kennedy and senior Foreign Office official Alexander Cadogan revealed a different calculation. Cadogan did not consider Britain automatically at war with the Soviet Union under its agreement with Poland. He said the Polish ambassador had requested a formal protest but had not asked Britain to declare war. The same report records rejection of Moscow’s claim that the Polish government had ceased to exist. British officials could reject the justification while declining to enlarge the war. [23] The terms of the British commitment help explain this response. Although the public Anglo-Polish agreement referred generally to aggression by a European power, its secret protocol defined that power, for the relevant obligation, as Germany. Megan Donaldson’s study of treaty secrecy establishes both the restriction and the fact that the protocol remained unpublished until 1945. Britain was therefore not treating its specific promise against Germany as an automatic declaration of war against every invader of Poland. That explains the scope of the obligation; it does not make the Soviet attack lawful or the British choice politically unavoidable. Cadogan’s conversation shows a government declining to extend an already dangerous war while maintaining that Poland continued to exist. [24] [23] Bullitt’s report of 20 September reveals French attention turning towards possible German offensives in western Europe and the danger to Romania. His account also conveyed expectations that the resources required for a successful offensive against Germany would take a prolonged period to assemble. These assessments are evidence of the assumptions organising French discussion, rather than reliable predictions of the war’s course. They expose the temporal disparity confronting Polish diplomacy: its government needed action within the remaining campaign, while Allied planning increasingly addressed the conflict that would follow Poland’s defeat. [25] France likewise remained at war with Germany without declaring war on the Soviet Union. Its position must be distinguished from the particular wording of Britain’s secret protocol. Bullitt’s dispatch exposes French fears about the next German offensive and southeastern Europe, rather than evidence of an imminent plan to relieve Poland from the Soviet attack. The Western governments’ continued recognition of Poland rejected Moscow’s argument of state extinction, but recognition and an additional military commitment were separate decisions. [25] [26] Romania faced the consequences at its own frontier. An American report of **20 September** recorded German pressure and Romanian restrictions on the Polish leadership that had crossed into the country. Officials were constrained in their communications, including the use of cipher, and the Romanian government resisted treating them as a functioning government merely passing through. Internment thus disrupted the Polish authorities’ attempt to continue their work abroad. It did not retrospectively validate the Soviet assertion, made before their departure, that the government had already vanished. The report also described efforts to arrange a constitutionally valid successor government in France. [27] Hungary, by contrast, offered routes through which refugees and soldiers could move, and its authorities tolerated assistance to men continuing towards the Polish forces abroad. That cooperation mattered because evacuation was becoming a military policy as well as an individual search for safety. Crossing into a non-belligerent country did not necessarily mean abandoning the war: the survival of trained personnel could sustain future units even after their formations inside Poland had disintegrated. Hungary’s help coexisted with its alignment towards Germany, underscoring the difference between a government’s broad diplomatic position and particular decisions taken at its borders. [28] Washington did not answer the invasion with military intervention. Its diplomatic reports followed the attack and the dislocation of Poland’s government while American neutrality remained in force. On **2 October**, Secretary of State Cordell Hull explicitly affirmed continued recognition of the Polish government despite the country’s subjection to force. This subsequent statement supplied an unambiguous answer to the Soviet legal pretext. It preserved diplomatic standing rather than territorial security, a distinction that Polish soldiers and civilians experienced far more urgently than foreign ministries did. [29] [26] At Brest on 22 September, German and Soviet commanders presided over a military ceremony as the German occupation gave way to Soviet possession. Heinz Guderian and Semyon Krivoshein appeared together there. The occasion made visible the cooperation described in the telegrams: the arrival of the second invading army could be arranged with the first, while the state whose territory they occupied had no voice in the transfer. [30] [26] Berlin, meanwhile, dealt with Soviet intervention as something to coordinate. The September correspondence does not depict two powers independently rescuing populations from an accidental collapse. It records negotiations over their respective operations and the settlement that would follow. On 19 September, Molotov told Schulenburg that the earlier possibility of retaining a reduced Polish state had given way to a preference for partition. Even after the invasion began, the precise political outcome was still being discussed. Agreement on destroying Poland’s freedom of action preceded agreement on every detail of the territory to be taken. [31]

The invasion becomes an occupation

The political programme had also begun before the frontier crossing. A Byelorussian Front directive dated 16 September instructed officials to create temporary administrations including army and NKVD representatives, organise newspapers and arrange the transfer of landed property. It explicitly postponed the creation of collective farms. This was preparation to replace existing authority and reshape society, with the pace of particular measures adjusted to the immediate situation. The instruction is a useful corrective to the suggestion that administration developed only as an improvised response to disorder after the troops arrived. [12] The protective language therefore addressed several audiences with related purposes. It supplied foreign governments with a diplomatic explanation, soldiers with an account of their mission, and selected inhabitants with expectations of social change. Army and political-police institutions would determine how those promises were translated into rule. Welcoming a particular measure gave local people no corresponding authority over the system imposing it. Conversely, avoiding combat offered no assurance against administrative coercion. The transition to occupation made these inequalities part of everyday life. The end of September would bring a revised German–Soviet boundary agreement, the subject of the next study. Its line should not be projected backwards onto 17 September as though every district had already changed hands that morning. Between the frontier crossing and the diplomatic settlement lay resistance, withdrawals, surrenders, captivity and decisions about escape. The distinction between those processes is the reason this atlas separates operational arrows from territorial boundaries. [32] The Soviet invasion joined military intervention to a claim that Poland had already ceased to exist. Advance orders and diplomatic coordination establish the preparation behind the action; continuing Polish resistance and political activity contradict the justification used to announce it. Their relationship explains why 17 September requires its own place in the chronology of partition. The attack closed possibilities of regrouping and escape while opening a new apparatus of coercive rule, and its effects depended both on decisions in Moscow and on the varied responses of soldiers, commanders and inhabitants within the invaded territory.
author: R.G. Cruise
location: Eastern Poland, Moscow and the European capitals
summary: Behind Moscow’s protective explanation stood a prepared offensive. Polish soldiers and civilians faced shrinking choices as Soviet formations advanced, resistance continued and promises of safety gave way to occupation.

sections.label: The Polish decision: fight, withdraw, or preserve the army
Lwów and the value of a promise

sourceMethod: Contemporary Soviet orders are read alongside German and American diplomatic reports, Polish military scholarship, museum research and testimony. Orders establish intended objectives, not actual daily positions. Transcriptions identify archival references but were not checked against original manuscript images. Reports and memoirs preserve particular perspectives; surveillance records are not opinion polls. Mick’s article is used only through its accessible abstract. Later battles are dated explicitly, uncertain casualty totals are omitted, and source notes record important limitations. Analysis connecting these findings is the atlas’s own interpretation.
